title: Given an array of numbers and a target, find all unique quadruplets that add up to the target. (LeetCode: 4Sum)
keyPoints: 4Sum extends 3Sum by adding one more fixed outer loop, giving two nested fix loops plus a two-pointer scan.
Sort the array first so duplicate skipping and two-pointer convergence both work correctly.
Skip duplicates at all four selection levels: outer loop, inner loop, left pointer, and right pointer.
Time complexity is O(n^3) because two loops each cost O(n) and the two-pointer scan costs O(n).
Use a wider numeric type like long for the running sum to avoid integer overflow when four values are large.
The same template generalizes to k-sum by recursively fixing elements until reaching the two-pointer base case.

s1_definition.oneliner: 4Sum finds all unique quadruplets in an array that add up to a target by sorting, fixing two elements with nested loops, and scanning the remaining two with a two-pointer technique.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **4Sum** – an extension of the 3Sum pattern where you fix one additional element with an outer loop before running the familiar two-pointer scan.
- **Sorting** – the array is sorted once so that duplicate values sit next to each other and the two-pointer convergence works.
- **Duplicate skipping** – at each of the four selection levels (outer index, inner index, left pointer, right pointer) you skip values equal to their predecessor to guarantee unique quadruplets.
- **Two-pointer scan** – after fixing two elements, the remaining two are found by moving a left pointer rightward and a right pointer leftward toward the target remainder.
- **Generalization** – the same skeleton extends to k-sum by recursively fixing elements and reducing the dimension by one until you reach the two-pointer base case.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh investigates structured transactions where exactly four payment amounts combine to hit an exact target figure. He lines up all the amounts in order, picks the first two amounts from the left, and then uses the two-pointer squeeze on the rest to find pairs that complete the target. He skips repeated amounts at every stage so no group of four is reported twice.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
4Sum Algorithm Flow
==================

Sorted array: [-2, -1, 0, 0, 1, 2]   Target: 0

  Fix i=0 (-2)
  ├── Fix j=1 (-1)         Need left+right = 3
  │   ├── left=2(0), right=5(2): sum=-1 < 0 → move left
  │   ├── left=3(0), right=5(2): sum=-1 < 0 → move left
  │   └── left=4(1), right=5(2): sum=0 == 0 → RECORD [-2,-1,1,2]
  │
  ├── Fix j=2 (0)          Need left+right = 2
  │   ├── left=3(0), right=5(2): sum=0 == 0 → RECORD [-2,0,0,2]
  │   └── left=4(1), right=4: left >= right → stop
  │
  └── Fix j=3 (0)          j=3 same as j=2 → SKIP duplicate

  Fix i=1 (-1)
  ├── Fix j=2 (0)          Need left+right = 1
  │   └── left=3(0), right=5(2): sum=1 > 0 → move right
  │       left=3(0), right=4(1): sum=0 == 0 → RECORD [-1,0,0,1]
  └── ...

Result: [[-2,-1,1,2], [-2,0,0,2], [-1,0,0,1]]


Duplicate Skip Points
=====================

  Level 1: i loop    → skip if amounts[i] == amounts[i-1]
  Level 2: j loop    → skip if amounts[j] == amounts[j-1] (within i)
  Level 3: left ptr  → skip past repeated values after recording
  Level 4: right ptr → skip past repeated values after recording


k-Sum Generalization
====================

  ┌──────────┐
  │  k-Sum   │  Fix one element, recurse on (k-1)-Sum
  └────┬─────┘
       │
  ┌────▼─────┐
  │ (k-1)Sum │  Fix one element, recurse on (k-2)-Sum
  └────┬─────┘
       │
       ...      (repeat until k=2)
       │
  ┌────▼─────┐
  │  2-Sum   │  Two-pointer scan on sorted remainder
  └──────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The 4Sum problem asks you to find every unique group of four numbers that adds up to a target, and the cleanest way to see it is as 3Sum with one extra fixed level on top. You sort the array once, use two nested loops to fix the first and second elements, and for each fixed pair you run the familiar two-pointer scan over the rest to find the remaining two elements that complete the target. The sorting is what makes both the two-pointer convergence and the duplicate skipping possible.

Duplicate handling happens at all four selection levels. At the outermost loop you skip a first element equal to the previous one, at the inner loop you skip a second element equal to the previous one within that iteration, and after recording a quadruplet you advance the left pointer past repeated values and retreat the right pointer past repeated values. Those four skips guarantee that every quadruplet you report is unique without storing results in a set for deduplication.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this pattern in the compliance team to detect structured transactions where exactly four payment amounts combined to hit an exact target figure. The team needed every unique quadruple so each case could be reviewed, and the sorted two-pointer approach found them in O(n^3) time instead of the O(n^4) brute force that would have been impractical at production volumes.

The senior-level insight is that this skeleton generalizes to any k-sum problem. You recursively fix elements and reduce the dimension by one until you reach the two-pointer base case, giving O(n^(k-1)) time. Always use `long` for the running sum to avoid integer overflow, and apply early termination pruning to skip iterations where no valid quadruplet can exist.

Remember one sentence: 4Sum is 3Sum with one extra fix loop on top, two-pointer scan for the last two, and duplicate skipping at all four levels.
